$comment: Build Spec §6: 'Policy levers have no equivalent source. Owner assigns, flagged as assigned.'
So every coordinate in this file carries kind:'assigned' and a `why`. None of it is derived,
and the product must render that distinction — a derived coordinate links to the agenda's own
stated assumption; an assigned one links only to us.
Lever set seeded from the 80,000 Hours US AI policy landscape (its enumerated policy tools:
testing and evaluation, industrial policy, R&D funding, regulations, export controls,
liability rules, insurance mechanisms, international agreements, compute governance, safety
evaluations) plus the institution-type taxonomy in the same article.
PLACEHOLDER STATUS: these twelve levers and their coordinates are our best reading, not the
owner's judgement. See OWNER-DATA.md item OD-07. The build does not block on it: the app runs
end to end on these and swaps them out when the owner's file lands.
Note on funding_government_usd (spec §9): government spend on a lever measures the size of the
PROBLEM, not the size of the safety response. It is a separate column, separately labelled, and
must never be summed with philanthropic funding into a composite.

institution_types.name: Executive Office of the President
institution_types.note: OSTP, NSC, OMB. ~10% political appointees; the rest career staff. Short-lived positions, high leverage, strong exit options.
institution_types.partisan_exposure: high for appointees, low for career staff

institution_types.name: Federal departments and agencies
institution_types.note: Implements through spending, R&D funding, export controls, technical standards and rule-writing. Formally nonpartisan civil service; slow, opaque hiring; clearances are durable career capital.

institution_types.name: Congress
institution_types.note: Holds the formal levers — budget, binding law, oversight. Staffers almost always work for one party, and that affiliation constrains later moves.

institution_types.name: State governments
institution_types.note: Faster, fewer veto points, precedent-setting (the 'California effect'). More accessible entry, quicker responsibility.

institution_types.name: Think tanks and advocacy
institution_types.note: Generate and communicate ideas, and act as talent pipelines into government. The article's own caveat: distance from decision-makers makes impact lumpy and hard to predict.
institution_types.partisan_exposure: varies from nonpartisan to explicitly ideological

levers.name: Testing, evaluation and standards
levers.one_sentence_summary: Build the state's ability to measure what frontier systems can do, and make those measurements count.
levers.theory_of_change: Credible third-party measurement → shared factual basis for regulation → rules that bind on capability rather than on vibes → earlier warning before a dangerous capability is deployed.
levers.why: Capacity-building rather than restraint by definition — it gives the state an instrument, it does not tell companies what they may do. Sits inside government because the measurement only counts if the measurer has standing. Nonpartisan enough that a career civil servant can hold it across administrations.

levers.name: Frontier model regulation and transparency mandates
levers.one_sentence_summary: Require frontier developers to disclose, to test before deploying, and to face consequences for not doing so.
levers.theory_of_change: Binding disclosure and pre-deployment obligations → internal safety work stops being discretionary → a floor under the race that does not depend on any one company's goodwill.
levers.why: The paradigm restraint lever. Presumes the binding constraint is will rather than knowledge — we largely know what we would want disclosed. Implies a low view of voluntary lab commitments, or the mandate would be redundant.

levers.name: Compute governance and export controls
levers.one_sentence_summary: Use the physical chokepoint — chips and datacentres — as the place where policy can actually bite.
levers.theory_of_change: Compute is countable, excludable and concentrated → tracking and controlling it is the one enforcement mechanism that does not require inspecting model internals → leverage over who gets to train frontier systems at all.
levers.why: Strongly interstate: export controls are an instrument of competition between states, and the lever only makes sense if you think that competition is where the risk sits. Requires being inside — the data and the authority are both government-held.

levers.name: Liability rules and insurance
levers.one_sentence_summary: Make developers internalise the cost of harm, and let insurers price the risk they will not disclose.
levers.theory_of_change: Clear liability → priced risk → an underwriting market that demands evidence of safety practices → private enforcement that scales without a regulator inspecting every model.
levers.why: Constrains companies, but indirectly — through price rather than prohibition, so it sits short of the frontier-regulation pole. Venue-neutral: liability has constituencies in both parties, which is unusual among these levers and is the reason it survives changes of administration.

levers.name: State technical capacity and talent
levers.one_sentence_summary: Get people who actually understand the systems into the rooms where decisions are made.
levers.theory_of_change: Technically literate staff inside government → definitions that survive contact with how models work → provisions that are enforceable → fewer rules that are either toothless or unworkable.
levers.why: The purest capacity lever, and the one the government disclaimer in spec §14 is written about. Deliberately low on venue_access: this is the lever that stays available to someone unwilling to foreclose partisan options, because technical competence in the room is a public good any administration benefits from.

levers.name: International agreements and diplomacy
levers.one_sentence_summary: Coordinate between states so that unilateral restraint is not simply unilateral disadvantage.
levers.theory_of_change: Shared standards and verification between the states that matter → restraint that does not hand the lead to whoever defects → a path out of the race that does not require anyone to trust anyone.
levers.why: The most interstate lever there is, and it presumes coordination rather than knowledge is what is missing. Low venue_access because diplomatic careers are built on continuity across administrations.

levers.name: Model weight security and infosec standards
levers.one_sentence_summary: Stop the weights from walking out of the building.
levers.theory_of_change: Security requirements proportionate to capability → frontier weights are not trivially stealable by state actors → the safety properties a developer builds in survive contact with the world.
levers.why: Mostly capacity — standards and clearances rather than prohibitions. Strongly deliberate-harm: the threat model is theft and misuse by an actor who knows exactly what they want. The least partisan lever in the set, which is why the job board shows a large infosec bloc.

levers.name: Misuse prevention: bio and cyber
levers.one_sentence_summary: Keep uplift for weapons of mass destruction out of generally available systems.
levers.theory_of_change: Screening obligations, capability thresholds and enforced safeguards at the point of synthesis and deployment → the marginal actor who could not build a weapon before still cannot.
levers.why: The clearest deliberate-harm lever in the set: nothing here is about a system pursuing goals nobody intended. Bipartisan in practice, so it stays open to someone unwilling to foreclose venues.

levers.name: Checks on power concentration
levers.one_sentence_summary: Keep advanced AI from becoming the instrument by which a small group stops needing anyone's consent.
levers.theory_of_change: Structural safeguards — on military and intelligence deployment, on chains of command, on who can direct systems at scale → no single actor acquires durable, unaccountable capability → the ordinary mechanisms of correction keep working.
levers.why: The domestic-concentration pole in lever form. Scores high on futures because the goal is not survival but retained influence over what happens next. Higher venue_access than its neighbours: this work is hard to do without taking positions that read as partisan.
example_bodies: Checks, Balances and Power Concentration work

levers.name: Industrial policy and public R&D
levers.one_sentence_summary: Spend public money to shape which capabilities exist and who has them.
levers.theory_of_change: Public compute, public datasets and directed research funding → safety-relevant research is not solely dependent on the labs → the state has an independent basis for judgement.
levers.why: Capacity, not restraint. Weakly lab-negative because the point is reducing dependence on lab-internal work for the field's evidence base.

levers.name: Incident reporting and emergency preparedness
levers.one_sentence_summary: Build the machinery to notice a serious failure and respond to it before the next one.
levers.theory_of_change: Mandatory reporting and a standing response capability → failures become visible and comparable → policy adjusts on evidence rather than on the news cycle, and the state can act inside the window that matters.
levers.why: Presumes containment is feasible — the whole lever is premised on catching something and acting in time. Mixed on restraint: reporting mandates constrain, response capability builds.

levers.name: Public understanding and advocacy
levers.one_sentence_summary: Change what the public and the press believe is at stake, so that the political window opens at all.
levers.theory_of_change: Sustained, accurate public argument → salience → political demand → the levers above become passable rather than theoretically available.
levers.why: The outside pole in its purest form, and it only makes sense if you think political will rather than technical knowledge is what is missing. High venue_access: advocacy that avoids ever taking a side tends not to move anything.
levers.caveat: Spec §13.6 applies most sharply here: returns to advocacy may increase rather than diminish. Being alone on an issue can mean being ignored rather than high-leverage.
